title: Algebra Foundations
description: Build confidence with variables, expressions, and simple equations through worked examples.
subject: Mathematics
licenseInfo: Original demonstration content written for EduSphere; no external textbook text or media is included.

chapters.title: Variables and expressions
objectives: Explain what a variable represents.
Write an expression from a short situation.
Evaluate an expression by substitution.

sections.heading: A letter can stand for a number
paragraphs: A variable is a symbol, often a letter, that represents a number. The value may be unknown or may change. In 3 + n, the letter n is the variable.
An algebraic expression combines numbers, variables, and operations. Unlike an equation, an expression does not contain an equals sign.
bullets: 5x means 5 multiplied by x.
x + 4 means four more than x.
2(a + 3) means twice the quantity a plus 3.

sections.heading: Translate a situation
paragraphs: Suppose a notebook costs p rupees. The cost of four notebooks is 4p rupees. If a student also buys a pencil for 6 rupees, the total is 4p + 6.

summary: A variable represents a number.
An expression has no equals sign.
Substitution means replacing a variable with its value and following the order of operations.

questions.prompt: A ticket costs t rupees. Which expression gives the cost of 3 tickets?
questions.explanation: Three groups of t rupees are written as 3t.

questions.prompt: Evaluate 2x + 5 when x = 4.
questions.explanation: Substitute 4 for x: 2 × 4 + 5 = 8 + 5 = 13.

chapters.title: Like terms and simplifying
objectives: Identify like terms.
Combine like terms using addition or subtraction.
Explain why unlike terms cannot be combined.

sections.heading: Group matching terms
paragraphs: Terms are separated by plus or minus signs. Like terms have the same variable part with the same powers. For example, 3x and 5x are like terms; 3x and 5y are not.
Imagine x as one kind of object. Three x-objects plus five x-objects make eight x-objects, so 3x + 5x = 8x. The coefficients add while the variable part stays the same.
bullets: 2x + 3y cannot be simplified by combining the terms.

sections.heading: Use the distributive property
paragraphs: Multiplication outside parentheses applies to each term inside. This is called the distributive property: k(a + b) = ka + kb.

example.title: Simplify an expression
steps: Combine the like terms 2x and x.

summary: Combine only terms with matching variable parts.
Add or subtract coefficients and keep the shared variable part.
Use distribution to remove a factor outside parentheses.

questions.prompt: Simplify 6y − 2y.
questions.explanation: Subtract the coefficients: 6 − 2 = 4, then keep y.

questions.prompt: True or false: 2a + 3b can be combined into 5ab.
questions.explanation: a and b are different variable parts, so the terms are unlike and cannot be combined by addition.

chapters.title: Solving one-step equations
objectives: Recognize an equation as a balance.
Use inverse operations to isolate a variable.
Check a solution by substitution.

sections.heading: Keep both sides balanced
paragraphs: An equation says that two expressions have the same value. Think of its equals sign as a balanced scale: doing the same operation to both sides keeps the balance.
Addition and subtraction undo each other. Multiplication and division undo each other. These are inverse operations.
bullets: If x + 7 = 12, subtract 7 from both sides.
If 4x = 20, divide both sides by 4.
Always check by putting the answer back into the original equation.

sections.heading: Solve and check
paragraphs: The goal is to leave the variable alone on one side. Use the inverse operation on both sides, then check whether the result makes the original statement true.

summary: An equation is a statement that two values are equal.
Apply the same operation to both sides.
Use inverse operations and check the answer in the original equation.

questions.prompt: Solve n − 4 = 9.
questions.explanation: Add 4 to both sides: n = 9 + 4 = 13.

questions.prompt: Solve 3x = 18.
questions.explanation: Divide both sides by 3. Then 3 × 6 = 18, so x = 6.

title: Geometry: Shapes and Measurement
description: Explore angles, perimeter, and area with clear diagrams described in words and worked examples.
subject: Mathematics
licenseInfo: Original demonstration content written for EduSphere; no external textbook text or media is included.

chapters.title: Angles and turns
objectives: Describe an angle as a turn between two rays.
Classify acute, right, and obtuse angles.
Use a straight angle and a full turn as reference points.

sections.heading: Measure a turn
paragraphs: An angle is formed when two rays share an endpoint called the vertex. The rays show the start and end directions of a turn. Angle size measures the turn, not the length of the rays.
A right angle is 90 degrees. An acute angle is smaller than 90 degrees. An obtuse angle is greater than 90 degrees but less than 180 degrees. A straight angle is 180 degrees.
bullets: A quarter-turn is 90°.
A half-turn is 180°.
A full turn is 360°.

sections.heading: Use known angles
paragraphs: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Angles around a point add to 360°. These facts help find an unknown angle when the other angles are known.

example.title: Find the missing angle on a line
steps: Two adjacent angles form a straight line, so their total is 180°.

summary: Angles measure turns and are measured in degrees.
Acute < 90°, right = 90°, obtuse is between 90° and 180°.
A straight line totals 180°; angles around a point total 360°.

questions.prompt: An angle of 35° is which type?
questions.explanation: 35° is less than 90°, so it is acute.

questions.prompt: Two angles on a straight line are 70° and x°. Find x.
questions.explanation: They add to 180°, so x = 180 − 70 = 110°.

chapters.title: Perimeter and distance around
objectives: Define perimeter.
Find the perimeter of polygons by adding side lengths.
Use units consistently.

sections.heading: Walk around the boundary
paragraphs: Perimeter is the total distance around a closed two-dimensional shape. Add the lengths of every outside side. Perimeter is measured in length units such as centimetres or metres.
A rectangle has two equal lengths and two equal widths. Its perimeter can be found as length + width + length + width, or 2(length + width).
bullets: Do not include interior lines.
Convert measurements to the same unit before adding.
Perimeter measures distance, not surface covered.

sections.heading: Calculate a rectangle's perimeter
paragraphs: For a rectangle with length 8 cm and width 3 cm, the boundary contains two 8 cm sides and two 3 cm sides.

summary: Perimeter is the total length of a shape's boundary.
Add all outside side lengths.
Use one consistent length unit.

questions.prompt: A square has side length 5 cm. What is its perimeter?
questions.explanation: A square has four equal sides, so 4 × 5 cm = 20 cm.

questions.prompt: A rectangle is 6 m long and 2 m wide. Find its perimeter.

chapters.title: Area of rectangles and triangles
objectives: Explain area as the amount of surface covered.
Calculate rectangle area using length × width.
Relate a triangle's area to a rectangle with the same base and height.

sections.heading: Count square units
paragraphs: Area measures the surface inside a two-dimensional boundary. It is measured in square units, such as cm². Covering a rectangle with unit squares shows why its area is length multiplied by width.
A triangle with a given base and perpendicular height has half the area of a rectangle with the same base and height.
bullets: Rectangle: area = length × width.
Triangle: area = ½ × base × perpendicular height.
Area uses squared units, unlike perimeter.

sections.heading: Compare two shapes
paragraphs: A rectangle 8 cm by 3 cm contains 24 square centimetres. A triangle with base 8 cm and perpendicular height 3 cm covers half that area.

example.title: Find a triangle's area
steps: Substitute base 8 cm and height 3 cm.

summary: Area measures the inside surface and uses square units.
Rectangle area is length × width.
Triangle area is half of base × perpendicular height.

questions.prompt: Find the area of a 7 cm by 4 cm rectangle.
questions.explanation: Area = 7 × 4 = 28 square centimetres.

questions.prompt: A triangle has base 10 cm and height 4 cm. What is its area?

title: Physics: Describing Motion
description: Understand distance, time, speed, and how motion can be represented with a simple graph.
subject: Physics
licenseInfo: Original demonstration content written for EduSphere; no external textbook text or media is included.

chapters.title: Distance and displacement
objectives: Distinguish distance from displacement.
Use a reference point to describe position.
Recognize that displacement includes direction.

sections.heading: Describe a journey
paragraphs: Distance is the total length of the path travelled. It is a scalar quantity: it has size but no direction.

Displacement describes the change from starting position to ending position along the shortest straight line, together with a direction. If a learner walks 3 m east and then 3 m west back to the start, the distance is 6 m but the displacement is 0 m.
bullets: Distance depends on the path taken.
Displacement depends on start and end positions.
Choose a reference point and state directions consistently.

sections.heading: Track a position change
paragraphs: On a straight east-west path, assign east as positive. A change from position 2 m to position 9 m gives a displacement of +7 m, meaning 7 m east.

example.title: Return to the start
steps: Walk 4 m north from the starting point.
Final position is 3 m north of the start, so displacement is 3 m north.

summary: Distance is total path length; displacement is directed change in position.
A round trip can have positive distance and zero displacement.
Direction matters for displacement.

questions.prompt: A person walks one lap and ends at the starting point. What is the displacement?
options: The lap length divided by time
questions.explanation: The starting and ending positions are the same, so the net displacement is zero.

questions.prompt: A student moves 5 m east then 2 m west. Give the displacement.
questions.explanation: Taking east as positive, the net change is 5 − 2 = 3 m east.

chapters.title: Speed and average speed
objectives: Define speed as distance per time.
Calculate average speed with consistent units.
Distinguish average speed from instantaneous speed.

sections.heading: Compare how fast journeys happen
paragraphs: Speed tells how much distance is covered per unit of time. Average speed equals total distance divided by total time. Common units include metres per second (m/s) and kilometres per hour (km/h).
Average speed uses the complete journey. It does not tell whether the object moved at that speed at every moment.
bullets: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Convert units before comparing values.
Speed has magnitude but no direction.

sections.heading: Calculate an average
paragraphs: If a cyclist covers 120 metres in 30 seconds, divide the distance by the time.

example.title: Find average speed
steps: The average speed is 4 metres per second.

summary: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Use consistent units and include the unit in the answer.
A journey's average speed may differ from its speed at a particular moment.

questions.prompt: A runner covers 60 m in 12 s. What is the average speed?
questions.explanation: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 metres per second.

questions.prompt: A vehicle travels 150 km in 3 hours. Find its average speed.

chapters.title: Reading distance-time graphs
objectives: Identify axes on a distance-time graph.
Interpret a horizontal line and a straight rising line.
Relate graph steepness to speed for a chosen scale.

sections.heading: Read the axes first
paragraphs: A distance-time graph shows how distance from a reference point changes as time passes. Time is normally on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis. Read the axis labels and scales before interpreting a point.
A horizontal segment means the distance stays unchanged during that time interval, so the object is at rest relative to the reference point. A straight rising line means distance increases steadily.
bullets: Check units and scale marks.
A steeper line means greater speed when the same axis scales are used.
A falling line may mean the object is getting closer to the reference point.

sections.heading: Use two graph points
paragraphs: The slope between two points on a distance-time graph represents the change in distance divided by the change in time, which is speed when direction is not being represented.

example.title: Read a straight segment
steps: Change in distance is 8 m and change in time is 4 s.
Speed on that segment is 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m/s.

summary: Time is usually on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.
A horizontal segment represents rest relative to the reference point.
For a straight segment, speed is change in distance divided by change in time.

questions.prompt: On a distance-time graph, what does a horizontal line show?
questions.explanation: Distance is not changing as time passes on a horizontal segment.

questions.prompt: Distance rises from 3 m to 15 m between 2 s and 8 s. Find the segment's speed.
questions.explanation: Change in distance is 12 m and time is 6 s, so speed is 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m/s.

title: Chemistry: Atoms and Elements
description: Learn how atoms, elements, and simple molecules describe the particles that make up matter.
subject: Chemistry
licenseInfo: Original demonstration content written for EduSphere; no external textbook text or media is included.

chapters.title: Inside an atom
objectives: Name protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Compare their charges and locations.
Relate atomic number to proton count.

sections.heading: Three subatomic particles
paragraphs: An atom has a small central nucleus and electrons around it. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. A proton has positive charge, a neutron has no electric charge, and an electron has negative charge.
In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the positive and negative charges balance. Most of an atom's mass is concentrated in its nucleus.
bullets: Proton: positive, in the nucleus.
Neutron: neutral, in the nucleus.
Electron: negative, around the nucleus.
Atomic number equals the number of protons.

sections.heading: Read a neutral atom
paragraphs: A neutral atom with atomic number 6 has six protons. Because it is neutral, it also has six electrons. Its number of neutrons depends on the isotope.

example.title: Count particles in a neutral atom
steps: Neutral means electrons equal protons, so it has 8 electrons.
Do not infer the neutron count without the isotope's mass number.

summary: The nucleus contains protons and neutrons; electrons occupy the surrounding region.
Protons are positive, neutrons neutral, and electrons negative.
Atomic number is the proton count; a neutral atom has equal proton and electron counts.

questions.prompt: Which particle has a negative electric charge?
questions.explanation: Electrons have negative charge.

questions.prompt: How many protons are in a neutral atom with atomic number 11?
questions.explanation: Atomic number is defined as the number of protons.

chapters.title: Elements and symbols
objectives: Define an element by its proton count.
Read common chemical symbols.
Explain why changing proton count changes an element.

sections.heading: One kind of atom
paragraphs: An element is a pure substance made of atoms that share the same number of protons. If the proton number changes, the atom is a different element.
Chemical symbols are short labels used worldwide. The first letter is capitalized; if there is a second letter, it is lowercase. For example, C is carbon and Ca is calcium.
bullets: H is hydrogen; O is oxygen; Na is sodium.
Capitalization matters: Co is cobalt, while CO is a formula with carbon and oxygen.
An element's identity is set by its proton number.

sections.heading: Read a symbol carefully
paragraphs: A symbol can represent one atom of an element. A small number written after a symbol in a formula counts atoms; it is not part of the element's symbol.

example.title: Read H₂O
steps: H is the symbol for hydrogen and O is oxygen.
The subscript 2 means two hydrogen atoms.
No subscript after O means one oxygen atom.
The formula describes one water molecule with two H atoms and one O atom.

summary: Elements contain atoms with the same proton number.
Symbols use a capital first letter and optional lowercase second letter.
Subscripts in formulas count atoms; capitalization changes meaning.

questions.prompt: Which symbol is correctly written for calcium?
questions.explanation: Element symbols capitalize the first letter and use a lowercase second letter.

questions.prompt: How many oxygen atoms are shown in CO₂?
questions.explanation: The subscript 2 applies to oxygen, so there are two oxygen atoms.

chapters.title: Molecules and simple formulas
objectives: Describe a molecule as bonded atoms.
Count atoms in a chemical formula.
Distinguish a coefficient from a subscript.

sections.heading: Atoms can join
paragraphs: A molecule is a group of atoms held together by chemical bonds. A molecule can contain atoms of one element, such as O₂, or different elements, such as H₂O.
A subscript applies to the element symbol immediately before it. A coefficient in front of a formula multiplies every atom in that formula.
bullets: O₂ contains two oxygen atoms in one molecule.
2H₂O means two water molecules: four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms in total.
A formula describes composition, not the size or shape of the particles.

sections.heading: Count the atoms
paragraphs: Read subscripts first, then multiply by any coefficient in front of the formula.

example.title: Count atoms in 3CO₂
steps: One CO₂ unit has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms.

summary: Molecules contain atoms joined by chemical bonds.
Subscripts count atoms in a formula; coefficients multiply the entire formula.
Count each element separately.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 2H₂O?
questions.explanation: Each H₂O has two hydrogen atoms; two molecules contain 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.prompt: How many total atoms are in one CO₂ molecule?
questions.explanation: There is one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms, for three total.

title: Biology: The Cell
description: Explore cells as living systems and learn the roles of the membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus.
subject: Biology
licenseInfo: Original demonstration content written for EduSphere; no external textbook text or media is included.

chapters.title: Cells: the basic unit of life
objectives: Describe a cell as a basic unit of living things.
Distinguish unicellular and multicellular organisms.
Use a microscope scale idea carefully.

sections.heading: Living things are made of cells
paragraphs: A cell is the smallest structure that can carry out the processes of life. Some organisms, such as many bacteria, consist of one cell. Plants, animals, and many fungi consist of many cells that work together.
Cells vary in shape and size. Their structures help them perform different roles. A drawing of a cell is a model, not an exact picture of every cell.
bullets: Unicellular means made of one cell.
Multicellular means made of many cells.
Cells are usually too small to see clearly without magnification.

sections.heading: Observe at different magnifications
paragraphs: A microscope makes a small object appear larger. Magnification does not change the object's actual size. A scale bar helps estimate the true size of structures in an image.

example.title: Compare two cell drawings
steps: Check whether both drawings show a scale bar.
If one image is enlarged more, its cell drawing may look bigger on the page.
Compare the scale bars or stated magnification rather than page size.
Describe the actual size only when the scale information supports it.

summary: Cells are the basic units that carry out life processes.
One-celled organisms are unicellular; many-celled organisms are multicellular.
Magnification changes apparent size, not actual size.

questions.prompt: An organism made of one cell is described as…
questions.explanation: The prefix uni- means one.

questions.prompt: Does increasing microscope magnification change an object's real size?
questions.explanation: Magnification changes how large the object appears, not its actual size.

chapters.title: Cell structures and their roles
objectives: Identify the cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus.
Summarize the role of each structure.
Recognize that plant cells have additional structures.

sections.heading: A cell has organized parts
paragraphs: The cell membrane forms a boundary around a cell and controls many substances entering or leaving. Cytoplasm is the material inside the cell where many chemical reactions take place. In many cells, the nucleus contains genetic material and helps coordinate cell activities.
Plant cells also have a cell wall outside the membrane. Many plant cells contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large permanent vacuole containing cell sap. Not every cell has every structure.
bullets: Membrane: boundary and selective exchange.
Cytoplasm: site of many reactions.
Nucleus: contains genetic material in many eukaryotic cells.
Plant cell wall: support; chloroplasts: photosynthesis; vacuole: cell sap storage.

sections.heading: Connect structure to function
paragraphs: A structure's position and materials often help it do its job. A boundary can separate the cell from its surroundings, while chloroplast pigments capture light energy.

example.title: Compare a plant and animal cell
steps: Both have a cell membrane and cytoplasm.
Many animal and plant cells have a nucleus.
Plant cells also have a cell wall; many have chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
Use the word 'many' or 'typical' rather than claiming every cell is identical.

summary: Cell parts have different roles that work together.
Plant cells have a cell wall; many also have chloroplasts and a large vacuole.
Descriptions should allow for variation among cells.

questions.prompt: Which structure controls many substances entering or leaving a cell?
questions.explanation: The cell membrane forms the boundary and regulates exchange with the surroundings.

questions.prompt: Which structure in many plant cells is the main site of photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Chloroplasts contain pigments that capture light for photosynthesis.

chapters.title: Cells with specialized jobs
objectives: Explain cell specialization.
Connect a cell's feature to its function.
Describe how cells can form larger structures.

sections.heading: Structure supports function
paragraphs: In multicellular organisms, cells can become specialized for particular functions. A red blood cell is adapted to carry oxygen; a root hair cell increases surface area for absorbing water and minerals; a nerve cell has an elongated shape for carrying signals over distance.
Specialization happens within an organized system: cells can form tissues, tissues form organs, and organs work together in organ systems.
bullets: A feature is useful when it helps the cell's job.
Not every cell has the same shape or contents.
The levels of organization are cell → tissue → organ → organ system.

sections.heading: Explain an adaptation
paragraphs: A good explanation links a feature to an effect and then to a function. Naming a feature alone does not explain why it is useful.

example.title: Root hair cell
steps: Effect: it provides a larger surface area in contact with soil.
Function: more water and mineral ions can be absorbed.
This links structure to the cell's role.

summary: Specialized cells have features suited to particular jobs.
Explain adaptation by linking feature, effect, and function.
Cells organize into tissues, organs, and organ systems.

questions.prompt: Why does a root hair cell have a long extension?
options: To increase surface area for absorption
questions.answer: To increase surface area for absorption
questions.explanation: The extension increases contact with soil for water and mineral uptake.

questions.prompt: Put these levels in order from smaller to larger: organ, cell, tissue.
questions.explanation: Cells group into tissues, and tissues form organs.

title: Computer Science: Problem Solving with Algorithms
description: Plan clear step-by-step solutions and use sequence, selection, and repetition to describe programs.
subject: Computer Science
licenseInfo: Original demonstration content written for EduSphere; no external textbook text or media is included.

chapters.title: Algorithms and clear instructions
objectives: Define an algorithm.
Write ordered, unambiguous instructions.
Test a procedure with an example input.

sections.heading: A plan a person or computer can follow
paragraphs: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of steps for completing a task or solving a problem. It describes the process, not necessarily a particular programming language.
Instructions should be precise enough that another person can follow them. State what information is needed, what action to take, and how to recognize the result.
bullets: Sequence matters: changing the order can change the outcome.
Avoid vague steps such as 'do it properly'.
Check that the procedure reaches an output for valid inputs.

sections.heading: Design a simple algorithm
paragraphs: Consider finding the total cost of two items when their prices are known. A clear plan identifies both inputs and performs the addition.

example.title: Add two prices
steps: For inputs 12 and 8, the output should be 20.

summary: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of instructions.
Precise steps and clear inputs make procedures testable.
Trace an example input to check the output.

questions.prompt: What is an algorithm?
options: A finite ordered set of steps
questions.answer: A finite ordered set of steps
questions.explanation: An algorithm gives ordered instructions to solve a problem or complete a task.

questions.prompt: Why should algorithm instructions avoid vague words like 'somehow'?
questions.answer: They must be precise and repeatable
questions.explanation: Precise instructions allow another person or computer to follow and test the same procedure.

chapters.title: Sequence and selection
objectives: Explain sequence as ordered steps.
Describe selection using a condition.
Trace a two-branch decision.

sections.heading: Choose a path with a condition
paragraphs: Sequence is the order in which instructions run. Selection chooses between actions based on a condition, often expressed as if/else.
A condition is a question that can be true or false. A program checks it and follows the matching branch.
bullets: If the condition is true, run the if branch.
Otherwise, an else branch can handle the other case.
Both branches should produce an appropriate result.

sections.heading: Trace a decision
paragraphs: A school activity might classify a score as pass or review. The threshold is part of the rule and should be stated clearly.

example.title: Classify a score
steps: If score is at least 40, display 'Pass'.
For score 52, the condition is true, so the output is 'Pass'.

summary: Sequence is instruction order.
Selection uses a true/false condition to choose a branch.
Test values on both sides of a threshold, including the boundary.

questions.prompt: Which programming structure selects between paths using a condition?
questions.explanation: Selection evaluates a condition and chooses a branch.

questions.prompt: For the rule 'if score ≥ 40 pass, otherwise review', what happens at score 40?
questions.explanation: The condition includes equality, so 40 meets the threshold.

chapters.title: Repetition and simple loops
objectives: Explain repetition in an algorithm.
Count iterations in a fixed loop.
Avoid an unchanging condition in a while loop.

sections.heading: Repeat without copying steps
paragraphs: A loop repeats a set of instructions. A fixed-count loop is useful when the number of repetitions is known. A condition-controlled loop continues while a condition remains true.
Loops reduce duplicated instructions, but the loop condition and update must be designed carefully. A condition that never becomes false can create an infinite loop.
bullets: A loop body contains the instructions repeated each time.
A counter can track the number of repetitions.
Update the counter or condition so the loop eventually stops.

sections.heading: Trace a counted loop
paragraphs: A loop that starts a counter at 1 and repeats while the counter is at most 3 will run for counter values 1, 2, and 3.

example.title: Count the repetitions
steps: Check count ≤ 3: true; perform the action.
Increase count by 1 and check again.
The action runs for 1, 2, and 3: three times total; at 4 the condition is false.

summary: Loops repeat instructions while a count or condition allows.
Trace each iteration, including the final condition check.
Ensure the loop can reach a stopping condition.

questions.prompt: A loop repeats for count values 1, 2, 3, and 4. How many times does its body run?
questions.explanation: There are four listed values, so the body runs four times.

questions.prompt: What can happen if a loop condition never becomes false?
questions.answer: It can become an infinite loop
questions.explanation: The program keeps repeating because the stopping condition is never reached.
